messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] SNP 6.0 arrays: CN probe locations
parts:
Hi,

the aroma.affymetrix UGP files contain the exact same genomic
positions as in the Affymetrix NetAffx CSV files. The positions are
unit by unit (locus), not probe by probe. See Section 'Resources' on
Page 'GenomeWideSNP_6'
[http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/genomewidesnp-6]
for further details and links on how the UGP files are created.

/Henrik

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: SNP 6.0 arrays: CN probe locations
parts:
On Mon, May 19, 2008 at 9:49 PM, Yu Chuan <mbc...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I checked the section
>
> # Import NetAffx CN probe position data
>
> Looks like it imports both 'chromosomeStart' and 'chromosomeStop'.
> But I still don't see how you define the position of each CN unit.
> Is it the middle point of 'chromosomeStart' and 'chromosomeStop'?

It is the readDataUnitChromosomePosition() of AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile
[see print(readDataUnitChromosomePosition.AffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile)]
that does the actual reading and specifies what and how it gets read.

The columns in the NetAffx CSV files keep changing between versions
[hence column name pattern
"^(physicalPosition|chromosomeStart|probeStartPosition)$" is used to
identify the position column regardless of version. In case there is
are 'chromosomeStart' and 'chromosomeStop' (as in the na24 version), I
decided to only read the former.

However, more details (that I forgot about). The actual "import" of
the above data to the UGP file, is done by
importFromAffymetrixNetAffxCsvFile() of AromaUgpFile. That one takes
an optional argument 'shift' which defaults to "auto". If "auto", the
value of 'shift' is inferred from the column names in the NetAffx CSV
file. It typically is shift=0, but if the column name for the
position match pattern "[sS]tart" it is shift=13. Thus, in the case
with GSW6 and na24, the position in the UGP file is indeed
chromosomeStart+13 (which of course relies on the assumption that the
probes are 25-mers).

I'm honestly curious, when will it be useful to have that precision of
location? I mean, the error in the location of a breakpoint found by
a segmentation algorithm will be greater than 13 bases. What's you
use case? ...or do you just want to make sure you know the details.

Cheers

Henrik
